feed.title: BHM 2026 Hub: what is new
feed.subtitle: Releases of the BHM 2026 Hub, with what changed and how it was checked

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.24.0
entry.summary: A new page, Beyond government, in the Lead menu: employers and supply chains, the voluntary, community and faith sector, funders, and trade unions and professional bodies (22 sourced points). Two new sections inside Life stages and identities: intersections for older, disabled and LGBT+ people (17 points) and place across the four nations and the regions (24 points). A new section inside The African diaspora on what governments in Latin America, Asia and the Middle East do on recognition, data and equality law (13 points). Every point independently re-read; corrections to three older points (pensioner low income, LGB+ identification, a bill to repeal the equality duty).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.23.0
entry.summary: A new page, Your profession, in the Practice menu: choose any of the 33 Civil Service professions or 13 government functions to see the hub sections with the most evidence for it and its official page, with what is published about ethnicity by profession (18 sourced points). Three new sections: science, engineering and the built environment (inside Innovation, 21 points), sport (inside Culture, 20 points) and uniformed and frontline public services (inside Representation, 22 points). Every point was re-read against its sources by an independent check before publication; points that could not be confirmed were left out (C168, D-139, D-140).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.22.0
entry.summary: Two new pages: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people (policy, service, content and data design; 23 sourced points) and Mixed heritage (the UK and around the world; 32 sourced points), each independently re-read before publication. A seventh menu, Practice, for the pages used at work. Help run the hub: a champion pack, champion and field review panel roles, contributors named by choice, ‘You said, we did’, and a contribution record mapped to the Civil Service behaviours. Review and assessment: a live coverage map of 96 fields, disciplines, functions, professions and sectors (C166, C167, D-132 to D-138).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.21.1
entry.summary: How the hub describes itself: a fuller description; on the website a canonical address, a card for when the link is shared, and linked data for search engines (the site and its open data); a data package describing every open data file.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.21.0
entry.summary: Calendar: events suggested on GitHub and accepted at triage join the calendar through a reviewed pull request, with the organiser’s page as the source; published award and nomination deadlines are now calendar entries, and subscribed calendars remind you 14 and 2 days before. Assurance: the latest result of each repository workflow, and a source freshness report giving every source’s read date and the date it is due to be read again. Help run the hub: express interest in volunteering in public on GitHub from any edition. A release feed (Atom) in the open data (C164, D-127 to D-130). Security: an independent review found that a crafted event link could have added script to a link; every source link is now escaped, community links must have a plain host name, and a new check fails if any element carries an inline handler (C165, D-131).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.20.0
entry.summary: Accessibility: the masthead logo, the futures quadrants, the network map and the knowledge-graph nodes now have accessible names that contain their visible text, including text shortened to fit (WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name; found by axe-core 4.14 in CI; C163, D-126). Calendar: five observance days and the New Cross remembrance now cite authoritative sources (UN, UN News, GOV.UK, The National Archives, UNESCO, George Padmore Institute), found by a new open-data validator (D-125). Repository: actions pinned to commit hashes, least-privilege tokens, OpenSSF Scorecard, a website health monitor, checks of the checks, a licence assessment, automatic releases with checksums and signed build attestations, release management, a wiki generated from the documentation, and discussion forms.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.19.1
entry.summary: Accessibility: charts and tables redrawn after start-up keep their keyboard tab stop when they scroll sideways (found by the new accessibility scan in CI on the volunteer-hours chart at phone width; C162, D-124).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.19.0
entry.summary: A user manual and a repository admin guide, linked from Help run the hub; standard community files (support, governance, accessibility, privacy, citation, changelog); an accessibility scan of every page and code scanning in CI; a 404 page, sitemap and security contact for the website.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.18.0
entry.summary: Privacy: the three downloadable Office templates carried a personal name in their document properties; they now carry only the hub’s name, and a scan of every embedded file guards against it. The public repository now builds and tests on any machine, with an admin guide, a user manual, community health files and accessibility checks in CI.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.17.1
entry.summary: In memoriam: a few words about the maker’s mother and about the women of the family, drawn from the family’s own archive and anonymised (no names, places, dates beyond the two already shown, occupations, migration details or health).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.17.0
entry.summary: Ideas, wishes and issues now flow through the public repository: the hub opens GitHub issue forms prefilled field by field (including the page), and on the public site the ideas box shows the ideas and feature wishes raised on GitHub, with their support and status, from a list a repository workflow publishes (no token in the page; unsafe items dropped, C161, D-123). Repository: issue triage with a privacy check, label sync, pull-request checks, a monthly link check and triage reminder, release packaging and Dependabot.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.16.1
entry.summary: The hub’s public repository is now github.com/cyberdudeuk/black-mixed-heritage: the issue, correction, idea and accessibility forms open there, and the GitHub Pages and Teams editions are built for it.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.16.0
entry.summary: Collecting ethnicity data, inside the language page: how UK guidance says to ask (the harmonised census question, self-description, prefer not to say, special category data, never inferring), when in a process to ask (application, shortlist, after award, registration), what stops people and organisations disclosing, and declaration rates across the Civil Service, NHS, law, research funding, honours, the arts, health records and policing (32 points).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.15.0
entry.summary: Recognition and representation, inside the culture page: how often Black and Black-Mixed people have won or been nominated for UK honours, military medals, Nobel and science prizes, learned-academy fellowships, research grants, scholarships, the Oscars, BAFTAs, Emmys, Tonys, the Booker, Mercury, Turner and Pulitzer prizes, and professional appointments, with a 68-row summary table of published counts and shares against population baselines; no person is classified by the hub (C160, D-121). Central Africa (Kongo, Ndongo, Loango, Kuba, Luba-Lunda, Bamum, Kanem-Bornu, Congolese rumba, the Congo Free State) and more Caribbean islands added to Black communities around the world; the Central Africa coverage floor restored to 2%.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.14.0
entry.summary: Black and Black-Mixed communities around the world, inside The African diaspora page: Latin America (the largest African-descended populations outside Africa: Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela, Central America and the Garifuna, Mexico, Argentina and Uruguay); continental Europe and Canada; African-descended communities in South Asia and the Middle East; the Caribbean beyond Jamaica; and where people of mixed heritage involving African ancestry are most numerous, country by country, with what genetic studies say and why the hub does not use the word ‘miscegenation’. Honouring our communities, inside the theme page: plaques, monuments and renamings, days of remembrance, museums and archives, honours and awards, with who does what, for whom, where and when, and the hub’s proposals by who acts. A global coverage audit on the review page sets floors for under-covered regions (C159).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.13.2
entry.summary: The hub is now credited only as made in a personal capacity: the author card, job titles, biography, place of birth, the author named in the footer, copyright line and linked data, and every reference to the author’s other projects (names on cards, the list of those projects, the reusable-ideas table and the companion-portal cross-check tables) were removed. Points that drew on that work now show as hub notes, with no figures.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.13.1
entry.summary: Privacy: the hub’s own privacy check had the very strings it guards against written into its code, visible to anyone reading the page source; it now uses general patterns instead. A note linking the Lusophone Africa entries to the author’s personal archival research was replaced: those entries rest on published scholarship.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.13.0
entry.summary: New page, Curriculum and reference works (Resources): the reference works that exist, from Du Bois’s Encyclopaedia Africana and Ghana’s 1962 project to the Dictionary of African Biography, UNESCO’s General History of Africa and the Oxford Companion to Black British History; where England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland stand, with both views on England’s review and its timetable (curriculum 2027, first teaching 2028); the evidence on who studies this history; and the hub’s proposals for a content framework and an open, UK-focused reference. Language of the time: 20 historical terms, from ‘half-caste’ and ‘West Indian’ to ‘BAME’ and South Africa’s ‘Coloured’, are explained instead of silently banned, and 98 quoted or named uses across the hub link to their explanation; works written to spread prejudice are still paraphrased (C158). Evidence: every claim that rested on one source now has a second; five unreadable sources replaced; weaker sources upgraded; the strip-search figure dated and explained; a Black Death event added for West Asia; corrections to iron-working, Songhai, Sankore, Mali, city-size and comparison wording; plain-http sources removed.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.12.0
entry.summary: New page, Who built the stereotypes, and what they cost (Learn): the philosophers, scientists, writers and officials whose work created or kept alive prejudiced ideas about Black, African, Caribbean and Mixed people, from Linnaeus, Hume and Kant to Gobineau, Galton, eugenics and the IQ hereditarians; the documented effects on schools (the ‘educationally subnormal’ placements, Rampton and Swann), immigration law, health care (pain, maternity, lung tests), policing of children and public attitudes; the Black writers and scholars who answered them, from Equiano and Cugoano to Firmin, Douglass, Du Bois and Diop; and how universities, science bodies and museums are facing that legacy. Only people who have died are named; disputed readings (Kant, Morton) give both views; every point has two independent sources. Food and heritage moved to This month.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.11.0
entry.summary: The features of the newer pages now reach the older ones: twenty more content pages open with ‘In short’, a plain-English summary whose every number is traced to the passage it links to, and end with ‘From where you stand’, suggestions for different readers linked to the passages behind them. Sections that cover the same ground on different pages now link to each other both ways (‘Also covered on other pages’), repeated passages were merged into one place with links from the others, and the menus put related pages side by side (What was taken and lost now follows Journeys of knowledge in Learn; The African diaspora sits beside What it means to be Black in Understand). A feature matrix on the review page shows which page has which feature. Evidence strengthened: 58 points on Journeys and What was taken that rested on Wikipedia alone now cite museums, universities, UNESCO or journals, which corrected 46 of them (for example the earliest Egyptian writing about 3320 BC, Meroitic deciphered in 1911, Trevor-Roper’s “unrewarding gyrations”, about 300,000 Timbuktu manuscripts saved); one unsupported quotation was removed. Twelve new world-timeline events give Central and Southern Africa maths, astronomy and medicine for the first time (Ishango, sona drawings, the Kongo dikenga, lukasa boards, Border Cave, the Pleiades and Canopus, buchu and hoodia) and add Asian medicine (Ge Hong, Chinese variolation, al-Razi). Privacy: notes naming the author’s role and private conversations were removed. Checks C153 to C157.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.10.0
entry.summary: World civilisations in parallel on the History page: 272 sourced events in 15 regions and 12 fields, side by side on one interactive timeline with filters, a play-through of time, a ‘meanwhile, around the world’ panel, a coverage grid and a table. Two new pages: Africa’s knowledge and its journeys (Learn), and What was taken, lost and might have been (Understand), with every point labelled as evidence, argument or counter-argument. A repetition audit blocks new content that repeats existing content. Fixes: page source lists stopped at S999 and missed most newer sources (C152); the calendar widened the page on Saturdays (C151); checks gather evidence faster. Theme moved to This month and Questions people ask to Resources.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.9.1
entry.summary: Tablets keep a navigation bar on its own full-width row, folding only what does not fit into ‘More’; on phones the menu opens as sections you can expand, and it scrolls within the screen (before, on a tablet, every group collapsed into one menu about 3,400px tall that could not be scrolled). A filter on one new page no longer hides cards on the others. Checks C147 and C148, plus navigation tests at five screen widths.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.9.0
entry.summary: Six new pages built from eleven research strands and checked against live sources: What it means to be Black (identity around the world and the African context in the UK); Black enterprise (seen from the community’s side); Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET; Representation across the state (ladders from entry to the top in government, Parliament, the courts and public services, with private offices); Through other lenses (responsible AI, data, history and public services); and the DEEIA lens (diversity, equity, equality, inclusion and accessibility), which also tags every card. Every point is sourced or marked as a hub note; each page has suggestions for different readers, linked to their evidence. Eight new checks (C138 to C145), each proven by a planted defect.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.8.1
entry.summary: The linked-data download (JSON-LD) now includes every dataset that says it is exported, among them the knowledge, language, peoples and DNA pages, with sources as citations; a check compares the export with the declarations (C137).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.8.0
entry.summary: New page, DNA, genomes and African ancestry: why Africa holds the most genetic diversity; the main projects (HapMap, 1000 Genomes, H3Africa and others); under-representation and its costs; health findings framed by ancestry, not race (sickle cell, APOL1, Duffy-null); what DNA shows about the trade in enslaved Africans; ethics (Henrietta Lacks, helicopter research). A full-width map on the peoples page (regions, islands, seas, peoples divided by borders). Gaps closed: Jamaica’s flag meanings, the Rift Valley, Africa’s share of world population (modelled), the ironworking debate and six more language terms; 42 points that rested on Wikipedia alone now have stronger sources, which also corrected details such as the width of the Strait of Gibraltar. African roots links join the Africa pages. Accessibility: the Cards or List switch is now one choice for screen readers; the A to Z tab wraps with the arrow keys. Faster start: scroll hints wait for idle time; the book club search waits for typing to pause. A GitHub Pages and Microsoft Teams edition is prepared (C131 to C136).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.7.0
entry.summary: New page, Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement. The scale of Africa’s linguistic, ethnic and genetic diversity; how North Africa, the Sahel, West, Central, East and Southern Africa, the Atlantic and Indian Ocean islands and the Mediterranean basin differ; the seas around the continent; how colonial borders were made and which peoples they divided, with the counter-view; displacement from the trades in enslaved Africans to today’s conflicts and disasters; a dated timeline; and myths tested against the evidence (C126 to C129). Also: editors’ working notes found in three entries on the knowledge page and two on the language page were removed or rewritten, and a new check scans every researched dataset for them (C130).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.6.0
entry.summary: New page, Words matter: race and ethnicity (what each means, how UK law, statistics and science use them, and which to use when); why Black and African are not interchangeable; 26 terms to avoid or use with care, with debated terms showing both views; principles. The hub’s own words were checked and corrected (for example ‘enslavers’, not ‘slave-owners’), and a language check now scans every page (C123 to C125).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.5.1
entry.summary: Fixes found by the full test suite: low-contrast counts on the selected inequality chip; the ideas form scrolled sideways on phones after a long page name was added. Also: the culture timeline and teaching panels are drawn once instead of on every keystroke; talent status labels show the status alone with dates beside them; speed figures on the Review page updated (2.3 s desktop, 8.1 s slow phone).

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.5.0
entry.summary: Gaps closed with re-checked sources: Gypsy, Roma and Traveller History Month and the Netherlands’ Black Achievement Month in the FAQ; the 2020 ministerial answer on Black British history in the curriculum; Ethiopia’s flag meanings from Britannica; Africa’s area and the True Size of Africa map; human origins (Smithsonian); Nok, Djenné, mbira (UNESCO 2020), sorghum (eastern Sudan, fourth millennium BC), the Vai syllabary (about 1833), Ndebele painting and Sundiata. Not found, so not published: why Jamaica’s flag has no red, Africa’s share of world population, a source naming the Rift Valley. Check C122.

entry.title: BHM 2026 Hub 2.4.1
entry.summary: Heavy pages (review, dashboards, knowledge graph) are drawn when first opened, and tooltips are added when the page is idle, for a faster start. Fixes from the code review: half the myth-or-fact quiz statements are now true; bingo printing waits for the print dialogue; dashboard bars are no longer tab stops; external links are checked and escaped; source references in tables are links; inequality chips show counts; ideas are saved one at a time and the owner can set each idea’s status; the self-report re-runs every routine; tooltips keep existing descriptions; tab sets support Home and End; AI suggestions retry if AI was still loading; larger header buttons and checkboxes; consistent menu highlight. Checks C121.
